Stuck in the mud of sensual desire means beings are caught and clinging in the mud that is called sensual desire.

The path leading to a bad destination means the path that goes to the states of loss, such as hell. Caused by sensual desire means caused by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. Many means of many kinds, divided into killing living beings and the rest. Bringing disease means that, in the sense of causing pain, they bring the suffering called disease, which is divided into what belongs to this present life and so on.

Thus refers to the manner already stated, beginning with "enemies, killers." Producing enmity means they give rise to a state of hostility. Tormenting means causing burning; the meaning is that they are scorching. Defiling means bringing defilement. The bait of the world means they are like bait in the world. Binding means they are to be bound by the fetters, which are like bonds; the meaning is that they lead to fetters. The bond of death means they are a bond of death because they are the cause of rebirth in the states of existence and so on, and because they keep the round going.

Maddening means that, through their nature to change and through separation, they produce the madness of grief; or, for one who is bound, they bring ever greater intoxication. Making one prattle means they make one babble on and on, "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!" There is also the reading "making one wag." <note>The following sentence is garbled in the printed text and the editor marks it with a question mark.</note> Like a dog wagging its tail for a lump of cooked rice, for the sake of bait they make beings fawn more and more, <unclear>knowing the highest state, did no evil; this is the meaning</unclear>. Agitating the mind means that, by producing feverish burning and so on, they habitually churn the mind both now and in the future. Or the reading is "crushing the mind." The meaning is the same. Those who say "making the mind heedless" take the meaning to be that they bring heedlessness of mind. For defiling means for oppressing or for tormenting. A net set by Māra means that these things called sensual desires should be regarded as a trap <note>the printed text here reads "uditaṃ kuminan," marked "(!)" by the editor; it is understood as a fish-trap set by Māra</note> spread out by Māra, because they bring ruin to beings.

With endless dangers refers to sayings such as "this is enticement and death." My defilements are burned away <note>original: "kilesā jhāpitā mayham"</note> and the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Having attained the state of an <term>Arahant</term> <gloss>a fully enlightened being</gloss>, she thought: "Now that I have reached the summit, what will I do by staying here? I will go to <term>Rājagaha</term> <gloss>the capital of Magadha</gloss> to pay respects to the Teacher, and many of my relatives will perform meritorious deeds." She returned to Rājagaha together with the other nuns. When <term>Visākha</term> <gloss>her former husband</gloss> heard of her arrival, he wished to test her spiritual attainment. He asked her questions regarding the five aggregates and other topics. <term>Dhammadinnā</term> answered every question as easily as if she were cutting a lotus stalk with a well-sharpened sword. Visākha reported the entire exchange of questions and answers to the Teacher. The Teacher praised her, saying, "The nun Dhammadinnā is wise, Visākha," and confirmed that her explanations aligned with his own omniscient knowledge. Using that discussion as the origin of the <term>Cūlavedalla Sutta</term> <gloss>The Shorter Series of Questions and Answers</gloss>, he appointed her as the foremost among the nuns who are preachers of the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>the Buddha's teachings</gloss>. At that time, while living in that village dwelling, she had attained the lower paths and established insight for the sake of the highest path. Then she spoke this verse:

One who has birthed a desire for the Final Goal, whose mind is permeated with it, and whose heart is no longer bound to sensual pleasures, is called "one who flows upward" and is set free.

In this context, "one who has birthed a desire" <note>original: "chandajātā"</note> means one who has developed a longing for the highest fruit of enlightenment. "For the Final Goal" <note>original: "avasāye"</note> refers to the end or the completion. Because her heart is not bound to sensual pleasures, she is called "one who flows upward," which refers to the completion of the monk's task for anyone. Therefore, through these two phrases, it is said that she is one who, though not yet having reached the very end, is striving for the supreme security from bondage. "Whose mind is permeated with it" means her mind should be touched by <term>Nibbāna</term> <gloss>the state of liberation</gloss> through the lower paths of the noble ones. "Whose heart is no longer bound to sensual pleasures" means that by the power of the path of the <term>Anāgāmī</term> <gloss>Non-Returner</gloss>, her mind is no longer attached to worldly desires. "One who flows upward" <note>original: "uddhaṃsotā"</note> means the stream of the path and the stream of existence flows upward...

"Now that I have attained Arahantship and reached the summit, what shall I do by staying here? I will go to Rājagaha itself, pay homage to the Teacher, and many of my relatives will make merit." With this thought she returned to Rājagaha together with the nuns. Visākha learned of her arrival. Having heard of it, and wishing to test what she had attained, he asked her questions about the five aggregates <note>the five <term>khandhas</term> <gloss>components of a person: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness</gloss></note> and related topics. Dhammadinnā answered each question put to her as easily as one cuts lotus stalks with a well-sharpened knife. Visākha reported the whole exchange of questions and answers to the Teacher. The Teacher praised her with words beginning "Wise, Visākha, is the nun Dhammadinnā." He declared that her answers agreed with his own omniscient knowledge. Taking this very occasion as the origin of the Cūḷavedalla Sutta <note>the "Shorter Discourse of Questions and Answers," Majjhima Nikāya 44</note>, he appointed her to the foremost place among the nuns who are preachers of the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>the Buddha's teaching</gloss>. Earlier, however, while she was living in that village dwelling, she had attained the lower paths and set out on insight meditation for the sake of the highest path. At that time

->She in whom desire has arisen, set on the end, and who has been touched by the mind,<-
->whose heart is not bound to sensual pleasures, she is called "one who goes upstream," and she is freed. 12.<-

she spoke this verse. Here, *she in whom desire has arisen* means one in whom desire has arisen for the highest fruit. *Set on the end* <note>original: "avasāye"</note>: the word <term>avasāya</term> means the end, the conclusion. Because the verse goes on to say "whose heart is not bound to sensual pleasures" and "one who goes upstream," this should be understood as the completion of the ascetic's task, whoever she may be. So with both expressions together the meaning is this: one whose mind has not yet attained, longing for the unsurpassed security from bondage <note>original: "anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ," a name for <term>Nibbāna</term> <gloss>the extinguishing of suffering</gloss></note>. *And who has been touched by the mind* means she would have touched, would have reached, <term>Nibbāna</term> through the minds of the lower paths. *Whose heart is not bound to sensual pleasures* means that, by virtue of the path of the <term>anāgāmī</term> <gloss>non-returner, the third of the four stages of awakening</gloss>, her heart is not bound to sensual pleasures. *One who goes upstream* means that the stream of the path, and the stream of rebirth too, carries her only upward

My defilements are burned away <note>original: "kilesā jhāpitā mayham"</note> and the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Having attained the state of an <term>Arahant</term> <gloss>a fully enlightened being</gloss>, she thought: "Now that I have reached the summit, what will I do by staying here? I will go to <term>Rājagaha</term> <gloss>the capital of Magadha</gloss> to pay respects to the Teacher, and many of my relatives will perform meritorious deeds." She returned to Rājagaha together with the other nuns. When <term>Visākha</term> <gloss>her former husband</gloss> heard of her arrival, he wished to test her spiritual attainment. He asked her questions regarding the five aggregates and other topics. <term>Dhammadinnā</term> answered every question as easily as if she were cutting a lotus stalk with a well-sharpened sword. Visākha reported the entire exchange of questions and answers to the Teacher. The Teacher praised her, saying, "The nun Dhammadinnā is wise, Visākha," and confirmed that her explanations aligned with his own omniscient knowledge. Using that discussion as the origin of the <term>Cūlavedalla Sutta</term> <gloss>The Shorter Series of Questions and Answers</gloss>, he appointed her as the foremost among the nuns who are preachers of the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>the Buddha's teachings</gloss>. At that time, while living in that village dwelling, she had attained the lower paths and established insight for the sake of the highest path. Then she spoke this verse:

One who has birthed a desire for the Final Goal, whose mind is permeated with it, and whose heart is no longer bound to sensual pleasures, is called "one who flows upward" and is set free.

In this context, "one who has birthed a desire" <note>original: "chandajātā"</note> means one who has developed a longing for the highest fruit of enlightenment. "For the Final Goal" <note>original: "avasāye"</note> refers to the end or the completion. Because her heart is not bound to sensual pleasures, she is called "one who flows upward," which refers to the completion of the monk's task for anyone. Therefore, through these two phrases, it is said that she is one who, though not yet having reached the very end, is striving for the supreme security from bondage. "Whose mind is permeated with it" means her mind should be touched by <term>Nibbāna</term> <gloss>the state of liberation</gloss> through the lower paths of the noble ones. "Whose heart is no longer bound to sensual pleasures" means that by the power of the path of the <term>Anāgāmī</term> <gloss>Non-Returner</gloss>, her mind is no longer attached to worldly desires. "One who flows upward" <note>original: "uddhaṃsotā"</note> means the stream of the path and the stream of existence flows upward...

### XV. THE DYAD OF TAINTS-WITH-OBJECTS

1. Dependent on a phenomenon that is a <term>taint-with-object</term> <gloss>something that can be the object of a taint</gloss>, a phenomenon that is a taint-with-object arises through root-condition.
Dependent on one aggregate that is a taint-with-object, three aggregates and mind-produced matter arise... and so on; for two aggregates... and so on. At the moment of rebirth-linking, dependent on the aggregates is the physical base; dependent on the physical base are the aggregates. Dependent on one great primary element... and so on; dependent on the great primary elements is mind-produced matter, kamma-born matter, and derived matter.

4. Dependent on a <term>taint-free</term> <gloss>something that cannot be the object of a taint</gloss> phenomenon, a taint-free phenomenon arises through root-condition.
Dependent on one taint-free aggregate, three aggregates arise... and so on; for two... and so on.

5. Dependent on a taint-free phenomenon, a taint-with-object phenomenon arises...
Dependent on taint-free aggregates, mind-produced matter arises.

6. Dependent on a taint-free phenomenon, both a taint-with-object and a taint-free phenomenon arise...
Dependent on one taint-free aggregate, three aggregates and mind-produced matter arise; for two... and so on.

7. Dependent on both a taint-with-object and a taint-free phenomenon, a taint-with-object <note>Manuscript B says: taint-free</note> phenomenon arises through root-condition.
Dependent on taint-free aggregates and the great primary elements, mind-produced matter arises. <note>This should be done just as the Worldly Dyad in the Lesser Intermediate Dyads; there is no difference</note>.

->The DYAD OF TAINTS-WITH-OBJECTS is finished.<-

The entire *Paṭṭhāna* is devoted, first to an inquiry into these twenty-four ways in which *x* is *paccaya* to *y* ; secondly, into illustrating how, in things material or mental, each kind of *paccaya* and groups of *paccayas* obtain. And here, in English, is the *Uddesa*, or statement of the twenty-four :

1. Condition, causal relation.
2. Object (presented to mind).
3. Dominance.
4. Contiguity.
5. Immediate contiguity.
6. Co-nascence.
7. Reciprocity.
8. Dependence.
9. Sufficing dependence.
10. Antecedence.
11. Consequence.
12. Habitual recurrence.
13. Action.
14. Result.
15. Support.
16. Control, faculty.
17. *Jhāna*.
18. Path, means.
19. Association.
20. Dissociation.
21. Presence.
22. Absence.
23. Abeyance.
24. Continuance.

To the modern reader there may seem not a little redundancy in this list. Buddhists themselves have thought so for centuries : 5 is treated as a variety of 4, 23 of 22, 24 of 21 ; 17 is a mode of 2. Others are the same relation considered with emphasis on either *x* or *y*—e.g., where *x* is antecedent, *y* is consequent (10, 11). And association, dissociation (19, 20) would by us be called a case of difference in likeness. Sufficing dependence is the supremely or sufficingly determining condition in a group of conditions or interdependence. And it is an interesting thing to find in a manual centuries later than Buddhaghosa, namely, the *Abhidhammattha sangaha*, that ‘all these 24 *paccaya’s* are reducible to Object (2), Sufficing dependence (9), Action (Karma, 13), Presence (21).’¹

### XV. THE DYAD OF TAINTS-WITH-OBJECTS

1. Dependent on a phenomenon that is a <term>taint-with-object</term> <gloss>something that can be the object of a taint</gloss>, a phenomenon that is a taint-with-object arises through root-condition.
Dependent on one aggregate that is a taint-with-object, three aggregates and mind-produced matter arise... and so on; for two aggregates... and so on. At the moment of rebirth-linking, dependent on the aggregates is the physical base; dependent on the physical base are the aggregates. Dependent on one great primary element... and so on; dependent on the great primary elements is mind-produced matter, kamma-born matter, and derived matter.

4. Dependent on a <term>taint-free</term> <gloss>something that cannot be the object of a taint</gloss> phenomenon, a taint-free phenomenon arises through root-condition.
Dependent on one taint-free aggregate, three aggregates arise... and so on; for two... and so on.

5. Dependent on a taint-free phenomenon, a taint-with-object phenomenon arises...
Dependent on taint-free aggregates, mind-produced matter arises.

6. Dependent on a taint-free phenomenon, both a taint-with-object and a taint-free phenomenon arise...
Dependent on one taint-free aggregate, three aggregates and mind-produced matter arise; for two... and so on.

7. Dependent on both a taint-with-object and a taint-free phenomenon, a taint-with-object <note>Manuscript B says: taint-free</note> phenomenon arises through root-condition.
Dependent on taint-free aggregates and the great primary elements, mind-produced matter arises. <note>This should be done just as the Worldly Dyad in the Lesser Intermediate Dyads; there is no difference</note>.

->The DYAD OF TAINTS-WITH-OBJECTS is finished.<-

### XV.
### THE DYAD OF WHAT IS WITH TAINTS

1. Dependent on a phenomenon with taints, a phenomenon with taints arises through root-condition.
Dependent on one aggregate with taints, three aggregates and mind-originated matter arise... and so on... dependent on two... and so on... At the moment of rebirth-linking, dependent on the aggregates, the physical base arises; dependent on the physical base, the aggregates arise. Dependent on one great element... and so on... dependent on the great elements, mind-originated matter, kamma-produced matter, and derived matter arise.

<note>The <term>khandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss> are the groups that make up a person. The <term>mahābhūtas</term> <gloss>great elements</gloss> are earth, water, fire, and air. <term>Paṭisandhi</term> <gloss>rebirth-linking</gloss> is the first moment of consciousness in a new life.</note>

4. Dependent on a phenomenon without taints, a phenomenon without taints arises through root-condition.
Dependent on one aggregate without taints, three aggregates arise... and so on... dependent on two... and so on...

5. Dependent on a phenomenon without taints, a phenomenon with taints arises...
Dependent on the aggregates without taints, mind-originated matter arises.

6. Dependent on a phenomenon without taints, phenomena both with and without taints arise...
Dependent on one aggregate without taints, three aggregates and mind-originated matter arise; dependent on two... and so on...

7. Dependent on a phenomenon with taints and a phenomenon without taints, a phenomenon with taints¹ arises through root-condition.
Dependent on the aggregates without taints and on the great elements, mind-originated matter arises. *(It is to be worked out just as the Mundane Dyad in the Lesser Intermediate Dyads²,³; there is no difference.)*

<note>The editors abbreviate here: the full set of conditional relations follows the same pattern as the earlier dyad on mundane and supramundane phenomena, so it is not repeated.</note>

->THE DYAD OF WHAT IS WITH TAINTS is finished.<-

## SECTION ON THE ANALYSIS OF CONDITIONS <note>original: <term>Paccayavibhaṅgavāra</term></note>

Preceding <note>The Siamese edition always uses the spelling <term>pūrimā</term>.</note> wholesome states <note>original: <term>kusalā dhammā</term></note> are related to subsequent wholesome states by way of the contiguity condition; they are related to neutral states <note>original: <term>avyākatānaŋ</term></note> by way of the contiguity condition.
Preceding unwholesome states are related to subsequent unwholesome states; they are related to neutral states by way of the contiguity condition.
Preceding neutral states are related to subsequent neutral states; they are related to wholesome states; they are related to unwholesome states by way of the contiguity condition.
Whatever states arise immediately after certain other states, the former states are related to the latter by way of the contiguity condition.

->5.<-

<note>The conditions for the immediate contiguity condition <note>original: <term>samanantarapaccayoy</term></note> are the same as those listed in section 4.</note>
Whatever states arise immediately after certain other states, the former states are related to the latter by way of the immediate contiguity condition.

->6.<-

The co-nascence condition <note>original: <term>Sahajātappaccayo</term></note> <gloss>arising together</gloss> means that the four immaterial aggregates <note>original: <term>khandhā</term></note> are related to one another by way of the co-nascence condition. The four great elements <note>original: <term>mahābhūtā</term></note> are related to one another by way of the co-nascence condition. At the moment of rebirth-linking <note>original: <term>okkantikkhaṇe</term></note>, mind and matter <note>original: <term>nāma-rūpaŋ</term></note> are related to one another by way of the co-nascence condition. Mind and mental factors are related to mind-produced matter. The great elements are related to derived matter <note>original: <term>upādā-rūpānaŋ</term></note> by way of the co-nascence condition. Material states <note>original: <term>rūpino dhammā</term></note> are related to immaterial states at certain times <note>The Burmese edition uses the spelling <term>kiñci kāle</term>.</note> by way of the co-nascence condition, and at other times not by way of the co-nascence condition.
